facts.title: The First Synthetic Transuranic
facts.text: Neptunium was the first element heavier than uranium ever created, synthesized in 1940 by Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson at the Berkeley Radiation Laboratory in California. They produced it by bombarding uranium-238 with neutrons, which captured a neutron and then beta-decayed into element 93. This discovery opened the door to the entire family of transuranic elements, and McMillan shared the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the work.

facts.title: Named for a Planet
facts.text: Neptunium is named after the planet Neptune, following the pattern set by uranium, which was named for Uranus. Because Neptune is the planet just beyond Uranus in the Solar System, it was the natural choice for the element that sits just beyond uranium on the periodic table. This celestial naming tradition continued with the very next element, plutonium, named for Pluto.

facts.title: A Surprisingly Dense Metal
facts.text: Pure neptunium is a silvery, lustrous metal that is remarkably dense, with the alpha form reaching about 20.45 grams per cubic centimeter, making it one of the densest of all the actinides. It melts at a relatively low 644 degrees Celsius and exists in three different crystal structures depending on temperature. Like many actinides, it is chemically reactive and slowly tarnishes in air.

facts.title: It Glows With Radioactivity
facts.text: All isotopes of neptunium are radioactive, with the longest-lived being neptunium-237, which has a half-life of about 2.14 million years. This isotope decays through a long chain of alpha and beta emissions, eventually ending at stable bismuth-209 (or thallium-205 by very recent measurements). Because of its long half-life, neptunium-237 is the form that accumulates and persists in nuclear waste.

facts.title: Hiding in Uranium Ore
facts.text: Although neptunium is essentially a man-made element, trace amounts occur naturally in uranium ores, formed when uranium atoms capture stray neutrons from natural fission and radioactive decay. These quantities are minuscule, measured in parts per trillion, far too small to mine. This makes neptunium one of the rarest naturally occurring elements on Earth.

facts.title: Fuel for Deep-Space Power
facts.text: Neptunium-237 can be irradiated with neutrons to breed plutonium-238, the isotope that powers radioisotope thermoelectric generators used on spacecraft. These generators turn the heat of radioactive decay into electricity and have powered missions like the Voyager probes, the Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers, and the New Horizons mission to Pluto. Thus neptunium plays a quiet but vital role in exploring the outer Solar System.

facts.title: It Can Sustain a Chain Reaction
facts.text: Neptunium-237 is fissile enough to sustain a nuclear chain reaction, and scientists have calculated its critical mass at roughly 60 kilograms in a bare sphere. In 2002, researchers at Los Alamos National Laboratory experimentally confirmed that neptunium can go critical, which is why the element is carefully tracked under international nuclear safeguards. Despite this capability, it has never been used to build a weapon.

facts.title: A Chemist's Color Palette
facts.text: In solution, neptunium can exist in an unusually wide range of oxidation states, from +3 all the way up to +7, and each state shows a distinct, vivid color. Neptunium(III) is purple, neptunium(IV) is yellow-green, neptunium(V) is green-blue, and neptunium(VI) is pink-red. This rainbow of oxidation states makes neptunium chemistry especially rich and a favorite subject for studying actinide behavior.

facts.title: The Neptunium Decay Series
facts.text: Neptunium-237 is the parent of one of the four major radioactive decay chains, known as the neptunium series. Unlike the other three chains, this series has largely vanished from nature because its longest-lived member decays far faster than the age of the Earth, about 4.5 billion years. Studying the surviving traces of this series helps scientists understand the history of radioactive elements in the cosmos.

facts.title: Captured in Tiny Amounts
facts.text: It took years after its discovery before anyone isolated a visible, weighable sample of neptunium metal, which was first prepared in 1944. Today a typical large nuclear reactor produces several hundred kilograms of neptunium-237 per year as a byproduct of uranium fuel. Managing this steady supply is a major challenge for nuclear waste storage, since its long half-life means it remains hazardous for over a hundred thousand years.
